issue.title: test_a_sleep_is_not_run_queue_wait reads ~0 elapsed under full-lane load

task_type_fields.evidence:
Observed in `sase tool run check` run f58662629c90d49036cf1eee012a7efc. The scoped lane
escalated to the full suite: 62375 passed, 2 failed, with load1 ~18 at start, a 19.1 GiB
tree RSS peak, and 14 pytest workers on a 64-core host. The agent was splitting
`tests/dev_update/test_progress.py`, which nothing imports, so the failure is not caused
by that diff.

Failure (`tests/test_sched_clock.py:17`, worker gw11):

    assert clock.elapsed() >= 0.045
    E  assert 0.00023539499257507757 >= 0.045

The node then passed 3/3 when re-run in isolation on the same unchanged tree. Fail rate:
1 of 1 full-lane runs, 0 of 3 isolated runs.

Suspected root cause (not yet verified): a read-order race in
`tests/_sched_clock.py::SchedulerAdjustedClock.elapsed()`. It computes
`wall = perf_counter() - started` first and only afterwards opens and reads
`/proc/thread-self/schedstat`. If the thread is preempted between those two reads, that
run-queue wait lands in `waited_now - waited` but not in `wall`. The clock then subtracts
time the wall window never contained, so `elapsed()` is understated, clamped at
`max(0.0, ...)`, and came out near zero here. A likely fix is to read schedstat before
`perf_counter()` in `elapsed()`, which only ever overstates elapsed by the
inter-read gap. `__init__` should keep its current wall-then-schedstat order. Confirm
by injecting a delay between the two reads before changing it, and check that the
latency-bound callers of the clock still hold.
task_type_fields.repro_cmd: sase tool run check (full lane under load)

issue.creation_reason: The scheduler-adjusted test clock reported 0.0002s for a 50ms sleep during a loaded full-lane check, then passed in isolation; a clock that understates elapsed time can also hide real latency regressions in the tests that rely on it.
